summary:
On the Moon there is no dusk. At the south pole the Sun skims just a few degrees above the horizon, so a ridge tens of miles away can cut a lander’s power for days. Earth can also drop out of sight and take communication with it. Move the landing a few hundred metres or a few days, and a mission can go from thriving to frozen.

HORIZON is a web app that turns this complexity into answers in seconds. Pick a historic or planned landing site, or enter your own coordinates, and watch the mission play out in 3D. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons, and the real horizon is computed from LOLA terrain. Countdowns to sunset and Earthset, a battery simulation and a success score show whether a site works on a given date. A calendar finds the best landing days, and scenario comparison answers the real planning question: slip the date or move the site? Pro mode adds charts, validation against NASA maps and custom lander specs. Luna, our AI guide, explains every result in plain language.

It’s built for everyone, from students to mission planners.
details:
HORIZON: see the Moon’s horizon before you land on it

What it does
HORIZON is a web app for evaluating lunar landing sites quickly. On the Moon, and above all near the south pole, the Sun skims a few degrees above the horizon. A distant ridge can therefore shade a lander for days, and Earth, the only direct communication link, can drop out of sight. HORIZON shows when and why this happens for any site and date, and how much it matters for the mission.

How it works

  1. Pick a site. Choose one of 19 curated sites (Apollo, Artemis III candidate regions, CLPS missions, Chandrayaan-3, Chang’e, SLIM) or enter custom coordinates. Map layers show slope, permanently shadowed regions, average sunlight and Earth visibility.
  2. Simulate. The backend gets Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons (DE441) every 10 minutes over 30 days. It builds a 360° terrain horizon out to 150 km from LOLA elevation data, including lunar curvature, and checks at every step how much of the solar disk and the Earth disk clears the terrain. The result is shown in a 3D scene and a 360° sky view, with countdowns to sunset and Earthset and an animated timeline.
  3. Model power and comms. A battery simulation charges in sunlight and drains in darkness. The default reference lander has power figures based on NASA’s VIPER rover, and users can enter their own specs. A transparent, weighted success score combines the lowest battery level, Earth visibility and the longest night. We also score the same mission with a flat horizon to show how much the real terrain costs.
  4. Compare. A calendar ranks landing days. Nearby search checks a 3×3 grid around the site. Scenario comparison answers the question planners actually ask: slip the date or move the site?
  5. Decide and explain. Pro mode adds charts, CSV export and validation against NASA PGDA illumination maps. The Mission Brief puts the decision on one printable page. Luna, our AI guide, explains results in plain language and tells the story of each site.

Benefits and impact
When a schedule slips or hardware changes, a team can evaluate plan B in minutes rather than days. Science and engineering teams get a shared view of the same data. Students, teachers and the public get an intuitive way to understand why landing near the lunar pole is so hard. The same tool is simple on the surface and deep underneath.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js with React Three Fiber, Zustand.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Rasterio/GDAL, HTTPX.
  • AI: a Qwen language model served through the Groq API.
  • Testing: pytest and Playwright.
  • Data: NASA JPL Horizons, LRO LOLA via NASA Moon Trek, NASA GSFC PGDA, LROC and NASA SVS imagery.
  • Development: we used an AI coding assistant (Anthropic Claude). No special hardware was needed.

What makes it creative

  • We turned raw ephemerides and elevation rasters into a visual story: watch the Sun disappear behind a real ridge 20 km away, then rewind the timeline.
  • Luna’s answers are grounded. Every number is computed by our backend, and the language model only narrates those facts, so the AI can’t invent results. Luna also jumps the timeline to the moment she is describing.
  • The flat-horizon comparison makes the value of real terrain data visible at a glance.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: real NASA data, with validation against independent PGDA maps.
  • Honesty about limits: the score is a heuristic, not a probability. Lander assumptions are visible and editable. Line-of-sight is the only communication factor modelled.
  • Accessibility: WCAG-level contrast, large tap targets, and status never shown by colour alone.
  • Reliability for live use: caching, request deduplication, timeouts and template fallbacks when the AI is offline.
  • Two audiences: a basic mode for newcomers and a Pro mode for experts.
